question_text: A 57-year-old man is brought to the physician for worsening mental status over the past 2 months. His wife reports he was initially experiencing lapses in memory and over the past 3 weeks he has begun having difficulties performing activities of daily living. Yesterday, he became lost heading to the post office down the street. He has hypertension treated with lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. Vital signs are within normal limits. He is alert but verbally uncommunicative. Muscle strength is normal. Reflexes are 2+ in bilateral upper and lower extremities. He has diffuse involuntary muscle jerking that can be provoked by loud noises. Mental status examination shows a blunt affect. A complete blood count and serum concentrations of glucose, creatine, and electrolytes are within the reference range. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

                    ### Question
                    A 57-year-old man is brought to the physician for worsening mental status over the past 2 months. His wife reports he was initially experiencing lapses in memory and over the past 3 weeks he has begun having difficulties performing activities of daily living. Yesterday, he became lost heading to the post office down the street. He has hypertension treated with lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. Vital signs are within normal limits. He is alert but verbally uncommunicative. Muscle strength is normal. Reflexes are 2+ in bilateral upper and lower extremities. He has diffuse involuntary muscle jerking that can be provoked by loud noises. Mental status examination shows a blunt affect. A complete blood count and serum concentrations of glucose, creatine, and electrolytes are within the reference range. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Alzheimer's disease
opb. Parkinson's disease
opc. Huntington's disease
opd. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
ope. Normal pressure hydrocephalus

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 57-year-old man presents with cognitive decline characterized by memory lapses, disorientation, and difficulties with daily activities, alongside involuntary muscle jerking and a blunt affect. His normal strength, reflexes, and lab results suggest a neurodegenerative disorder. Alzheimer's disease is common in this age group and aligns with the progressive nature of his symptoms. Parkinson's disease is less likely due to the absence of rigidity and tremor. Huntington's disease is unlikely given the age of onset and symptom profile, while Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease typically presents with more rapid progression and severe cognitive decline. Normal pressure hydrocephalus is also less likely due to the absence of gait disturbances. Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is Alzheimer's disease, supported by the consensus that it is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder in older adults.
